title: Gāyatrī Mantra
essence: May the radiance of the divine light up our minds.
devanagari:
तत्सवितुर्वरेण्यं
भर्गो देवस्य धीमहि ।
धियो यो नः प्रचोदयात् ॥
iast:
tat savitur vareṇyaṃ
bhargo devasya dhīmahi |
dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt ||

words.meaning: of Savitṛ, the divine impeller (the sun)
most excellent, worthy to be chosen

translation: May we meditate upon that most excellent radiance of the god Savitṛ, who may inspire our thoughts.
context: Attributed to the sage Viśvāmitra and composed in the gāyatrī metre of three eight-syllable lines. The opening “oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ” heard in daily recitation comes from later liturgical practice and is not part of the Ṛgveda verse itself.

title: Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Mantra
essence: Free me from fear of death, as a ripe fruit slips from its vine.
devanagari:
त्र्यम्बकं यजामहे
सुगन्धिं पुष्टिवर्धनम् ।
उर्वारुकमिव बन्धनान्
मृत्योर्मुक्षीय मामृतात् ॥
iast:
tryambakaṃ yajāmahe
sugandhiṃ puṣṭivardhanam |
urvārukam iva bandhanān
mṛtyor mukṣīya māmṛtāt ||
translation: We worship the three-eyed one, fragrant, who increases nourishment. Like a cucumber from its stem, may I be released from death, not from immortality.
context: Attributed to the sage Vasiṣṭha and addressed to Tryambaka, identified with Rudra–Śiva. The same verse also appears in the Yajurveda. It is recited for healing, protection and freedom from fear.

title: Ā No Bhadrāḥ
essence: Let noble thoughts come to us from every side.
devanagari:
आ नो भद्राः क्रतवो यन्तु विश्वतो
ऽदब्धासो अपरीतास उद्भिदः ।
देवा नो यथा सदमिद्वृधे असन्
अप्रायुवो रक्षितारो दिवेदिवे ॥
iast:
ā no bhadrāḥ kratavo yantu viśvato
'dabdhāso aparītāsa udbhidaḥ |
devā no yathā sadam id vṛdhe asann
aprāyuvo rakṣitāro dive-dive ||
translation: May auspicious thoughts come to us from every side, unharmed, unhindered, breaking through. May the gods be with us always for our growth, unfailing protectors, day after day.
context: The opening verse of a hymn to all the gods (Viśvedevas). Its first line, “let noble thoughts come to us from every side”, is widely quoted as a call to stay open to wisdom from anywhere.

title: Ekaṃ Sad Viprā Bahudhā Vadanti
essence: Truth is one; the wise call it by many names.
devanagari:
इन्द्रं मित्रं वरुणमग्निमाहु-
रथो दिव्यः स सुपर्णो गरुत्मान् ।
एकं सद्विप्रा बहुधा वदन्त्य-
ग्निं यमं मातरिश्वानमाहुः ॥
iast:
indraṃ mitraṃ varuṇam agnim āhur
atho divyaḥ sa suparṇo garutmān |
ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanty
agniṃ yamaṃ mātariśvānam āhuḥ ||
translation: They call it Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni; it is also the heavenly, fair-winged Garutmān. Reality is one; the wise speak of it in many ways. They call it Agni, Yama, Mātariśvan.
context: From the long riddle-hymn of the seer Dīrghatamas. The line “ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti” is among the most quoted in the Veda, often read as a statement that one reality is approached through many names.

title: Asato Mā Sad Gamaya
essence: Lead me from darkness to light.
devanagari:
असतो मा सद्गमय ।
तमसो मा ज्योतिर्गमय ।
मृत्योर्मामृतं गमय ॥
iast:
asato mā sad gamaya |
tamaso mā jyotir gamaya |
mṛtyor mā amṛtaṃ gamaya ||
translation: Lead me from the unreal to the real. Lead me from darkness to light. Lead me from death to immortality.
context: Part of the pavamāna chants in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. The Upaniṣad itself explains each line: the unreal is death, darkness is death, and all three lines are a prayer to move from mortality to immortality.

title: Pūrṇam Adaḥ
essence: From the whole, the whole arises, and the whole remains.
devanagari:
ॐ पूर्णमदः पूर्णमिदं
पूर्णात्पूर्णमुदच्यते ।
पूर्णस्य पूर्णमादाय
पूर्णमेवावशिष्यते ॥
iast:
oṃ pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idaṃ
pūrṇāt pūrṇam udacyate |
pūrṇasya pūrṇam ādāya
pūrṇam evāvaśiṣyate ||
translation: That is whole; this is whole. From the whole, the whole comes forth. Taking the whole from the whole, the whole alone remains.
context: Opens the fifth chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad and is also recited as the peace invocation (śānti mantra) of the Īśa Upaniṣad. It points to a fullness that nothing can add to or take from.

title: Īśā Vāsyam
essence: All this is filled with the Divine. Enjoy, but do not grasp.
devanagari:
ईशा वास्यमिदं सर्वं
यत्किञ्च जगत्यां जगत् ।
तेन त्यक्तेन भुञ्जीथा
मा गृधः कस्यस्विद्धनम् ॥
iast:
īśā vāsyam idaṃ sarvaṃ
yat kiñca jagatyāṃ jagat |
tena tyaktena bhuñjīthā
mā gṛdhaḥ kasya svid dhanam ||
translation: All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is pervaded by the Lord. Find joy through letting go. Do not covet, for whose is wealth?
context: The first verse of the Īśa Upaniṣad, which forms the fortieth chapter of the Śukla Yajurveda. Gandhi said that if all the Upaniṣads were lost and only this verse survived, it would be enough.

title: Uttiṣṭhata Jāgrata
essence: Arise, awake, and learn from the great.
devanagari:
उत्तिष्ठत जाग्रत
प्राप्य वरान्निबोधत ।
क्षुरस्य धारा निशिता दुरत्यया
दुर्गं पथस्तत्कवयो वदन्ति ॥
iast:
uttiṣṭhata jāgrata
prāpya varān nibodhata |
kṣurasya dhārā niśitā duratyayā
durgaṃ pathas tat kavayo vadanti ||
translation: Arise! Awake! Approach the great and learn. Like the sharpened edge of a razor, hard to cross, is that path, so the wise declare.
context: Part of Yama's teaching to the young seeker Naciketas. Swami Vivekananda made its opening words a rallying call: “Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached.”

title: Satyam Eva Jayate
essence: Truth alone triumphs.
devanagari:
सत्यमेव जयते नानृतं
सत्येन पन्था विततो देवयानः ।
येनाक्रमन्त्यृषयो ह्याप्तकामा
यत्र तत् सत्यस्य परमं निधानम् ॥
iast:
satyam eva jayate nānṛtaṃ
satyena panthā vitato devayānaḥ |
yenākramanty ṛṣayo hy āptakāmā
yatra tat satyasya paramaṃ nidhānam ||
translation: Truth alone triumphs, not falsehood. By truth the divine path is laid out, by which the sages, their desires fulfilled, ascend to where the supreme treasure of truth abides.
context: Its opening words, “satyameva jayate”, are the national motto of India, inscribed beneath the Lion Capital emblem.

title: Mātrā-sparśās Tu Kaunteya
essence: Heat and cold, joy and sorrow: they come and go. Endure them.
devanagari:
मात्रास्पर्शास्तु कौन्तेय
शीतोष्णसुखदुःखदाः ।
आगमापायिनोऽनित्याः
तांस्तितिक्षस्व भारत ॥
iast:
mātrā-sparśās tu kaunteya
śītoṣṇa-sukha-duḥkha-dāḥ |
āgamāpāyino 'nityās
tāṃs titikṣasva bhārata ||

words.meaning: contacts of the senses with their objects

translation: O son of Kuntī, the contacts of the senses with their objects bring cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go; they do not last. Endure them patiently, O Bhārata.
context: Spoken by Kṛṣṇa to Arjuna early in the Gītā's second chapter, as he begins to steady Arjuna's grief on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra.

title: Na Jāyate Mriyate Vā
essence: The Self is never born and never dies.
devanagari:
न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन्
नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः ।
अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो
न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
iast:
na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin
nāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ |
ajo nityaḥ śāśvato 'yaṃ purāṇo
na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||
translation: The Self is never born, nor does it ever die. Having come to be, it will never cease to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.
context: Kṛṣṇa's teaching on the deathless Self (ātman), given to free Arjuna from fear and grief. A close parallel appears in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad.

title: Karmaṇy Evādhikāras Te
essence: Your right is to the work, never to its fruits.
devanagari:
कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते
मा फलेषु कदाचन ।
मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूः
मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि ॥
iast:
karmaṇy evādhikāras te
mā phaleṣu kadācana |
mā karma-phala-hetur bhūr
mā te saṅgo 'stv akarmaṇi ||

words.meaning: the fruit of action as your motive

translation: You have a right to your actions alone, never to their fruits. Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, and do not cling to inaction.
context: Perhaps the most quoted verse of the Gītā, at the heart of its teaching on karma yoga: acting fully and well, without anxiety about the outcome.

title: Yadā Yadā Hi Dharmasya
essence: Whenever goodness fades, I rise.
devanagari:
यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य
ग्लानिर्भवति भारत ।
अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य
तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥
iast:
yadā yadā hi dharmasya
glānir bhavati bhārata |
abhyutthānam adharmasya
tadātmānaṃ sṛjāmy aham ||
translation: Whenever there is a decline of dharma and a rise of adharma, O Bhārata, then I bring Myself forth.
context: Kṛṣṇa reveals the purpose of divine descent (avatāra). It continues directly into the next verse, 4.8, on protecting the good.

title: Uddhared Ātmanātmānam
essence: Lift yourself by yourself. You are your own best friend.
devanagari:
उद्धरेदात्मनात्मानं
नात्मानमवसादयेत् ।
आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुः
आत्मैव रिपुरात्मनः ॥
iast:
uddhared ātmanātmānaṃ
nātmānam avasādayet |
ātmaiva hy ātmano bandhur
ātmaiva ripur ātmanaḥ ||
translation: Lift yourself up by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is its enemy.
context: From the Gītā's chapter on meditation (dhyāna yoga). It places responsibility for growth firmly in one's own hands.

title: Ananyāś Cintayanto Mām
essence: To those who are wholly devoted, I bring what they lack and keep what they have.
devanagari:
अनन्याश्चिन्तयन्तो मां
ये जनाः पर्युपासते ।
तेषां नित्याभियुक्तानां
योगक्षेमं वहाम्यहम् ॥
iast:
ananyāś cintayanto māṃ
ye janāḥ paryupāsate |
teṣāṃ nityābhiyuktānāṃ
yoga-kṣemaṃ vahāmy aham ||

words.meaning: gaining what is lacking and keeping what is gained

translation: Those who worship Me, thinking of no other, ever steadfast: for them I carry what they lack and preserve what they have.
context: A verse of assurance from the Gītā's chapter on the royal knowledge (rāja-vidyā). “Yoga-kṣemaṃ vahāmy aham” is the motto of the Life Insurance Corporation of India.

title: Sarva-dharmān Parityajya
essence: Take refuge in Me alone. Do not grieve.
devanagari:
सर्वधर्मान्परित्यज्य
मामेकं शरणं व्रज ।
अहं त्वा सर्वपापेभ्यो
मोक्षयिष्यामि मा शुचः ॥
iast:
sarva-dharmān parityajya
mām ekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja |
ahaṃ tvā sarva-pāpebhyo
mokṣayiṣyāmi mā śucaḥ ||
translation: Setting aside all duties, take refuge in Me alone. I will free you from all sins. Do not grieve.
context: Often called the culminating verse (carama-śloka) of the Gītā, spoken near the very end of Kṛṣṇa's teaching to Arjuna.

title: Bhaja Govindam
essence: Grammar rules won't save you at the end. Turn to Govinda.
devanagari:
भज गोविन्दं भज गोविन्दं
गोविन्दं भज मूढमते ।
सम्प्राप्ते सन्निहिते काले
नहि नहि रक्षति डुकृञ्करणे ॥
iast:
bhaja govindaṃ bhaja govindaṃ
govindaṃ bhaja mūḍhamate |
samprāpte sannihite kāle
nahi nahi rakṣati ḍukṛñ karaṇe ||

words.meaning: the grammar rule “ḍukṛñ, in the sense of doing”

translation: Worship Govinda, worship Govinda, worship Govinda, O foolish mind! When the appointed hour arrives, memorised rules of grammar will surely not save you.
context: Traditionally attributed to Ādi Śaṅkarācārya, who, legend says, composed it on seeing an old scholar memorising grammar rules. Its playful refrain makes it a favourite for singing.

title: Nirvāṇa Ṣaṭkam
essence: I am not the mind, not the senses. I am consciousness and bliss.
devanagari:
मनोबुद्ध्यहङ्कारचित्तानि नाहं
न च श्रोत्रजिह्वे न च घ्राणनेत्रे ।
न च व्योम भूमिर्न तेजो न वायुः
चिदानन्दरूपः शिवोऽहं शिवोऽहम् ॥
iast:
mano-buddhy-ahaṅkāra-cittāni nāhaṃ
na ca śrotra-jihve na ca ghrāṇa-netre |
na ca vyoma bhūmir na tejo na vāyuḥ
cid-ānanda-rūpaḥ śivo 'haṃ śivo 'ham ||

words.meaning: of the nature of consciousness and bliss

translation: I am not the mind, intellect, ego or memory; not the ears or tongue, nor the nose or eyes; not space, earth, fire or air. I am consciousness and bliss. I am Śiva, I am Śiva.
context: A six-verse hymn of Advaita Vedānta traditionally attributed to Ādi Śaṅkarācārya. Each verse negates what the Self is not and ends with the same refrain.

title: Śiva Tāṇḍava Stotram
essence: The drum thunders as Śiva dances the cosmic Tāṇḍava.
devanagari:
जटाटवीगलज्जलप्रवाहपावितस्थले
गलेऽवलम्ब्य लम्बितां भुजङ्गतुङ्गमालिकाम् ।
डमड्डमड्डमड्डमन्निनादवड्डमर्वयं
चकार चण्डताण्डवं तनोतु नः शिवः शिवम् ॥
iast:
jaṭāṭavī-galaj-jala-pravāha-pāvita-sthale
gale 'valambya lambitāṃ bhujaṅga-tuṅga-mālikām |
ḍamaḍ-ḍamaḍ-ḍamaḍ-ḍaman-ninādavaḍ-ḍamarvayaṃ
cakāra caṇḍa-tāṇḍavaṃ tanotu naḥ śivaḥ śivam ||

words.meaning: a garland of a great serpent

translation: His neck made pure by the streams flowing from the forest of his matted hair, a great serpent hanging there as a garland, his drum resounding “ḍamaḍ ḍamaḍ”, Śiva danced the fierce Tāṇḍava. May he grant us auspiciousness.
context: Traditionally attributed to Rāvaṇa, the scholar-king of Laṅkā, and famous for its thundering rhythm. Small spelling variants exist between printed editions; check this line against your chosen edition.

title: Liṅgāṣṭakam
essence: I bow to the liṅga of Sadāśiva, worshipped by all the gods.
devanagari:
ब्रह्ममुरारिसुरार्चितलिङ्गं
निर्मलभासितशोभितलिङ्गम् ।
जन्मजदुःखविनाशकलिङ्गं
तत्प्रणमामि सदाशिवलिङ्गम् ॥
iast:
brahma-murāri-surārcita-liṅgaṃ
nirmala-bhāsita-śobhita-liṅgam |
janmaja-duḥkha-vināśaka-liṅgaṃ
tat praṇamāmi sadāśiva-liṅgam ||
translation: The liṅga worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu and the gods, pure, radiant and resplendent; the liṅga that ends the sorrow born of birth: to that liṅga of Sadāśiva I bow.
context: An eight-verse hymn (aṣṭakam) sung widely in Śiva temples. It is popularly attributed to Ādi Śaṅkarācārya, though that attribution is uncertain.
